utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record all the accused are here. I don't notice any absences amongst the Defence teams. And from the Prosecution, I see Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Nicholls. And no one else. Good afternoon again. Mr. -- I don't know who to address but I suppose Mr. Nicholls. You are aware that an urgent motion, joint Defence motion, was filed earlier on today, seeking certification of our yesterday's oral decision relating to Witness 128 [Realtime transcript read in error "PW-128"] and the postponement of the testimony of the same witness. Since the motion is not only declared to be urgent but in itself is urgent, you're asked to respond to it now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, Your Honour. I've looked through the motion and my response in short is that I don't believe that the Defence have met the cumulative prongs of Rule 73(B) and I ask the Court to exercise its discretion to deny the motion. The main reason for my position is that the Defence's arguments about how this going forward will affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings and all these dire predictions of what may result seem to me to be purely speculative and not grounded. There is no reason to believe at this stage that the witness would have to be recalled or that a cross-examination will be longer. I don't see how that has been established. And if that's the case, the postponement would be for no reason at all so I don't think that they've met that expeditious and fairness prong. And the same goes for whether or not the credibility of the witness, they will be able to challenge that. Without going into the substance again of the underlying court's decision, I think that the Defence is able with the information provided to do a full and fair cross-examination. Should it turn out that there is any reason why further questions are required, the Court has built in a remedy which is to recall the witness, if necessary, if cause is shown. And I think that that is -- takes away any danger of unfairness or prejudice to the Defence and that it would be wrong to now send a witness home who has been here for a week, postpone all of this on the mere speculation that it may turn out that there may be additional questions that they need to ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does anyone of you wish to respond to the Prosecution reply? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have nothing to add to my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyone else? None? Okay. We'll come back with our decision later. In the meantime, let's proceed with this witness. How much more time do you need, Mr. Krgovic? Mr. Stojanovic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think about 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who else will be cross-examining this witness? All right. So our intention today was to have just one break, since we will be adjourning at 6.00, between 6.00 and 6.15 anyway, so we will need time in any case to go back to our Chambers and discuss the motion, the joint Defence motion. So we'll come back to you later on to tell you what is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your cross-examination. Mr. Stojanovic will be proceeding with his questions. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We were able to see two video clips or excerpts from the video clips, and you were able to five some people. Now I would like to revisit that and I would like to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is P02047, Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit, that's video clip V0004458. And the time is 1.54.45 through 55.09.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the video clip where you were able to recognise yourself is in fact part of this recording?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. The video was stopped at 1 hour 55 minutes 08 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanojevic, the persons that we can see on this recording, the civilians, they reached this hard-top road and they are heading toward the UNPROFOR base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you know this area, from what direction did they come from as they headed towards the UN base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what direction, to the right, there is this village of Budak. There is also the village of Gornji Potocari and a number of hamlets. I'm not able to tell you their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, in those villages, Budak, Gornji Potocari, there were no members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that you're saying, "Don't be afraid." That's what you're saying on this recording; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean when you were saying those things to those civilians?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I addressed them with the best of intentions. I saw that these women were scared. I told them not to be afraid, that they were free to go because this woman was crying. They wanted to pass through to the UN base. So I acted in the best of intentions, and I talked to them and I told them that they could pass through and that there would be no problems, and that is indeed how it was. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who is this man or the camera-man or the reporter to your right on this recording?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now just look at the following frame and then that's the end of the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the reason for looking for the following frame, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to hear the sentence and the -- you will see the translation of those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, and that's at 1.55.10 on this video recording, either you or somebody else standing next to you said, "Why did you leave, then?"

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know who said it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't, because there were quite a few of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not be needing this video recording any more but I would like to ask you in your estimate, and you actually did mark these locations, how far is this location where this recording was made from the location where the people of Srebrenica gathered in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 100 to 150 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this period that you told us was between one and two hours that you spent in Potocari on that date, you did not see any buses driving the civilians away in the direction of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And your departure from this area, as you indicated, was at any rate before the evacuation started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is our argument that no members of the PJP company that you were a part of did not take part in the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Bratunac. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will agree with you. We were in Bratunac at the department store when the first vehicles with the civilians started getting out, when the evacuation started with the first vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you headed from Potocari to Bratunac, you had to pass through in your vehicle across the Yellow Bridge and the UN observation post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at that time, as you were heading from Potocari towards the department store in Bratunac, so that's the 12th of July, that again you did not have any contacts with the UN troops and that your unit did not disarm any of them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, in the afternoon, you headed towards Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And on your arrival in the village of Sandici, you were deployed along the road and I wanted to ask you, the location that you marked on the aerial photograph, how far is it from the Kravica village or, rather, from the warehouse in the village of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about one kilometre, maybe a bit more, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what unit was deployed down along the road to your right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think there were some troops there but I can't really tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were some troops on the same side that you were, are you referring to the Republika Srpska army troops?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were some Republika Srpska army troops. I didn't recognise the soldiers and they didn't wear the same kind of insignia that the police wore or the Special Police Brigade wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the distance from that location in Sandici to Srebrenica is about ten kilometres as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the town itself to Sandici, there is about 10 kilometres. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Sandici and Vojnici [phoen] is in the area that was controlled by the Republika Srpska army in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the attack on -- in the night between the 12th and the 13th of July by the members of the 28th Division, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at Defence Exhibit 4DP1829, pages 27 to 28, in the B/C/S version. The translation is already in e-court and if we could look at -- that's 4D00108. That's page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The exhibit number is 4DP1892.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As we wait for this document to come up, I would like to tell you that this is an extract from the protocol book of the Bratunac health care centre, and we would be looking for the entries for the 13th of July 1995. Thank you. Could we perhaps scroll down a little bit? That's enough. Thank you very much. Mr. Stanojevic, you mentioned a member of your unit whose name was Zeljko Ninkovic. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, under 1471 [as interpreted], and the date is the 13th of July 1995, and the time is 4.45, it says here that a member of the Special Police from Zvornik was brought in from the area around the village of Kravica to the Bratunac health care centre, and here there is an indication that he was showing no signs of life. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that correspond to what you were testifying yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That precisely corresponds to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, line 21 on the previous page, page 8, you say, "Here, under 1471". From what I see it's 1481. Unless I'm looking at the wrong entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. Thank you very much. That's 1481. So could we have that correction for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanojevic, the next name is Nenad Andric, and again, his record is entered here under 1482 and it's recorded here that he was brought there that morning as a member of the Special Police from Zvornik from the Kravica area, and it is indicated -- his injuries are described here. Now, my question to you is whether Nenad Andric was wounded in that attack too?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know their names but I do know that three, I think my colleagues from Zvornik, were wounded and I think these are the people mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we then move on to the next page, that's page 3 in the English, and page 28 in B/C/S? It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The English document has only two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then it's page 2 of the English document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanojevic, again, under number 1483 and 1484, it is stated that on the 13th of July 1995, at 4.45, two people were brought to the health care centre in Bratunac, as Zarko Radic and Nenad Filipovic also members of the Special Police from Zvornik and their injuries are described here. It is also indicated that they sustained those wounds in the area of Kravica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would we agree that this actually confirms what you were saying yesterday that three people were wounded and this one man was killed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you left this area on the 13th of July, did you personally receive any instructions as to how you were to treat prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not and neither did the colleagues from my squad, from-- or rather people from the Bratunac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in the end let me just ask you, you know Ljubomir Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, he was your commander in the police station in Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1993, in fact, the paramilitary units from Bratunac attacked the police station in Bratunac and on that occasion the building sustained some damage and Ljubomir Borovcanin himself was attacked in the police station?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that but I was not in the station at that time. I remember, though, the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. What was the ethnicity of these paramilitary units that attacked the police station in Bratunac in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, since you have heard of this event, could you please tell us what was the ethnic background of the paramilitaries that attacked the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean Serbs from Serbia or Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these members of the paramilitary units from Serbia and from Bosnia or from Serbia or from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were some people from Serbia there but mostly they were Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that this attack on the police station, and on the authorities, was in fact repelled thanks to the citizens of Bratunac who joined in to defend the police station and gave their support to the police?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few citizens there. I don't know how many of them. I came later once the attack was already over. We were called in to go there and I spent the entire night there at the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the employees in the police station in Bratunac and the citizens of Bratunac towards Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had a lot of respect, both as a man and as a commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in the field often together with Ljubomir Borovcanin and the Special Police Brigade carrying out various tasks?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. We sometimes encountered each other in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever able to observe or to hear of any illegal orders issued by Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISAV STANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask again -- I had some indication previously that the Beara, Miletic, Popovic, Nikolic, Gvero and -- not Gvero and Pandurevic, wished to cross-examine this witness. Do you wish to cross-examine this witness? Mr. Zivanovic has already indicated that he doesn't. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We also don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Haynes, that you don't wish to cross-examine this witness. Okay. But is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Stanojevic, we don't have any further questions for you, which means that your testimony finishes here. Our staff will assist you to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and on behalf of everyone else I also wish you to -- I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Documents? Mr. Thayer? You circulated already a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the list consists of only the exhibits that were marked in court, and that do not appear in the still photo book which is an exhibit to an extent which is being filled as we go along through the trial with identifications from other witnesses. In other words, this witness identified a number of video stills which are in that still book. We will not be tendering those particular photographs at this point because we'll wait until later on in the trial when we've identified as many of those photographs as we can, and then offer the full book at that time. Therefore, the only remaining exhibits on this list are those stills which weren't in that video still book plus whatever was marked in court. That's why it's considerably shorter than the previous list we distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. We have received a copy of the list. Is there any objection from any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's first see whether there is any -- there are any objections to the admission of these documents. We hear none. The thing is, Mr. Thayer, we are making verifications actually at the moment but I'm being told that the book, the album of the stills, some of which were made use of yesterday, hasn't been MFI'd as yet. I'm not in a position to confirm or deny that, because I'm taken by surprise as much as all of you presumably are. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that may actually be the case. We've certainly referred to the book during the course of the examinations and in exchanging the exhibit or distributing the exhibit lists and so forth. For the record, it's P01936. It is in e-court. And we have referred to portions of that so far during the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From what we can see, for the time being at least, is that this document that is 1936 was not used, for example, with Mr. Ruez, and it was not tendered with the witness -- with the evidence of Mr. van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you will need to attend to this because it can create administrative problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would suggest perhaps that we do offer it right now, marked for identification, and then we'll proceed as we have, whatever we establish through the testimony of witnesses, we'll offer at the end and whatever is not, we'll excise from the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any objection from any of the Defence teams to have it tendered now and marked for identification? We hear none. Anyway, these are documents that will be made use of in due course for sure by both sides. And they have already been made use of. So that will be the case. So in addition to the documents that we have dealt with today, you will include this one, Madam Registrar. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position, and I thank Judge Kwon for taking the trouble to go back in time, searching, is that indeed during the testimony of Mr. van Duijn, you did refer the witness to 1936, saying, "I am going to be referring to various video stills which are contained in 65 ter 1936. It's a book of still images from the trial video which I believe was distributed to Your Honours and to Defence counsel as well." But in actual fact it was never tendered to be marked for identification, not even on that occasion. So I think we've solved the matter now. Again, thank you, Judge Kwon. Thank you, Mr. Thayer, and also the Defence teams for their cooperation. Mr. Stojanovic, do you wish to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just one, which is the book of protocol of the health centre in Bratunac. It already exists and has been used as 4DP01829 [sic], and we have also used it with another witness. Now we would like to have it admitted as a Defence exhibit. We want to use one part of the English translation, 4D00108. And I have just been told that the number that I have just quoted for the B/C/S version, 4DP01892, this is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1892 or 1829? Because in line 24, it's 1829. Line 3, it's 1892. And previously, I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is 1892, that that's the correct number, should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On page 8, line 7, it was also 1829. Now you're maintaining that it is 1892? Is it correct, 1892? All right. So whenever in the transcript we have 1829, that should be corrected and changed into 1892. I thank you for that clarification, Mr. Stojanovic, because otherwise we would have had a confusion. And to be precise, you're referring to two pages from that document where we have the entries that, 1481 to 1484, correct? Okay. Thank you. Any objection on your part, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that document is so admitted. There wasn't any other cross-examinations. So we can close this chapter here. I think we will now need to withdraw to have consultations on the urgent joint Defence motion and the response. We'll come back to you as soon as we are ready. I can't anticipate how long, but I don't anticipate it to be longer than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We intend to come back in roughly 20 minutes' time. --- Break taken at 3.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm loath to do this but there is no one here representing General Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to cover for them whilst Your Honour gives this judgement. No, seriously. It's something that happens commonly in my jurisdiction. I'm quite happy to cover for my English colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a way how we could check? All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, don't do it again. Yes. Here is our decision. It's an oral decision. Reasons will follow in a written decision. Our decision, having considered the joint Defence motion and the oral reply of the Prosecution is to dismiss the motion and to proceed therefore with the testimony of Witness 128. I apologise if previously I referred to him as Witness PW-128; it's just Witness 128. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before the witness is brought in, Your Honours, I wanted to raise the issue of Rule 90(E). Out of an abundance of caution, it might be advisable to advise the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there are no protective measures in place, are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to welcome you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require from you to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. The text is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn confirmation and undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Acimovic. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat. I'll explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. Mr. Nicholls for the Office of the Prosecutor will be putting some questions to you, after which he will be followed upon cross-examination by the various Defence teams. I don't expect your testimony to finish today, possibly not even tomorrow. There is one thing that I need to alert you to, hoping that this has already been mentioned to you and that you are aware of its import. There is a possibility that in the course of your either examination-in-chief or cross-examination, questions are put to you which, if answered, might tend to incriminate you. I don't know if this will happen or not, but in case such questions are put to you, you have a right under our rules to draw to our attention this and to ask to be exempted from answering such questions. This is not an absolute rule, however. We, the Judges composing this Trial Chamber, the four of us, after hearing submissions, have -- can decide either to grant you the exemption that you may request or not to grant you the exemption. If we grant you the exemption, obviously you don't answer that question or those questions. If we don't grant you the exemption, that means that we will be compelling you to answer those questions, which you will need to do. However, if you are so compelled to make statements in reply to questions put to you, whatever you say in that reply shall not, according to our rules, be used as evidence against you in any subsequent Prosecution that might be taken against you, unless we are talking of false testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of this right before? Had you been made? Were you made aware of this right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partially. In any case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So I think we can start with the testimony. Mr. Nicholls? He's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Srecko Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber when you were born, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you are a Bosnian Serb by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What is your present occupation? What do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I work in the catering industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I want to ask you now are some questions about your military background. Could you very briefly, for the Judges, outline your military career from 1992 through the beginning of 1995? Just the positions you held.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: When the war started in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means as of 1992, I was a foot soldier. I believe that in August 1992, I became a company commander. In November 1992, pursuant to an order of the brigade commander, I was appointed the commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. I remained in that position up to 1995, i.e., until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the name of that battalion change over time, and what was the name of the battalion you commanded in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, the unit changed its name. The 2nd Infantry Battalion was its name in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where was the command? Where was the headquarters of the 2nd Battalion in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Malesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In July 1995, where was your family home? Where were you living when you weren't at the command?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just so we know, approximately how far was the headquarters in Malesici from Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Some 14 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in July 1995, did Rocevic fall within the area of responsibility of the 2nd Battalion or would the 2nd Battalion be the battalion that would deal with any military problems in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which battalions would have been the ones to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Look here, I've told you -- actually, I told you last time that I believe that the village of Rocevic did not belong to any defence sector of any of the infantry battalions, in light of the fact that the defence sector of infantry battalions was usually ranging between three and five kilometres. In any case, the village of Rocevic was located in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade, and that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about a person named Drago Nikolic. Did you know an officer named Drago Nikolic in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: The assistant brigade commander for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, speaking of the time period before July 1995, could you just briefly describe your professional relationship with Drago Nikolic, how it went when you worked with him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a fair relationship, the relationship between me and Drago Nikolic, when it came to our cooperation and our duties. We never had any disagreements, so I would say that it was a fair relationship, a correct relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of personal relationship with him? Did you ever have drinks with him or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, we spent a lot of time together. The war went on for a few years. I suppose we did socialise here and there. We would have a drink together, and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know an officer named -- a VRS soldier or officer named Milorad Trbic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I came to know him in 1992, I believe, when they moved into Zvornik. He was assigned to my unit as a foot soldier. I'm talking about the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you still know him in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recall what his position was at that time?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was one of Drago Nikolic's assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to now direct your attention and ask you some questions about events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I get his rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness's rank or Mr. Trbic's?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness's.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us your rank in July 1995 when you were battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was a reserve lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you ask Mr. Trbic's rank as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Trbic's rank in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was also reserve lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about the days soon after the fall of Srebrenica or the liberation of Srebrenica, those events. Do you remember - and it's okay if you don't - but do you remember the approximate date of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, in the month of July, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At about the time of the fall of Srebrenica and the days afterwards, can you briefly tell us what kind of combat tasks were facing your battalion, what you were most occupied with?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: We were mostly occupied with the fortification of the front lines of our positions there. While this was going on, we had to move the front lines of our defence of the infantry company and the defence line was moved to provide for better tactical positions in front of the Serbian villages of Vitinica and Odzacina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And during this time, after the fall of Srebrenica, the week following, did you become aware of any prisoners being held in the area of the brigade, the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During the days following the fall of Srebrenica did you become aware of prisoners being held anywhere in the area of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, in my previous statements, I learned about prisoners being held in the village of Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber how you learned that information, who you learned it from, how you came to learn that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: One of those days, I went home just briefly to take a bath. I left my unit sometime around 2000 hours. I'm talking about the period between 2000 and 2100 hours. When I came home and did what I had come to do, in my family house I was visited by the priest of the Rocevic local commune and the president of the Rocevic local commune. They asked me if I had any information about prisoners who were in the gym of the Rocevic elementary school. Since I had never heard of those prisoners before, I was taken back by that question, and when they briefly informed me about what this was all about, together with them I went to the Rocevic school, and there I convinced myself that there were indeed prisoners there in the gym of that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us -- well, first of all, when the president of the local commune and the priest came to you, did they say anything about these prisoners, what they thought about these prisoners being held in the school? What was their feeling about that?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Rather uncomfortable. They also told me that a woman had been wounded not far from the elementary school, and that there was a lot of panic going around all day in the part of the village where the school was, in view of the events that were going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the woman who was injured, did you learn where that woman was from? And what I mean was: Was that a prisoner or was that a local person? Who was the woman?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: That woman was also a Rocevic local. She had been standing in front of her family house. She had been washing dishes at a well, and she was hit and wounded there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear for the record, I think your answer was clear but hit and wounded by what? What hit her?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: A sort of infantry weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you mean that she was physically hit with a weapon or hit with a bullet from an infantry weapon?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: A bullet, in any case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As best you can, from what you remember, can you describe the scene at the school when you got there, who you saw, what you saw going on?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I arrived in front of the elementary school, I saw unknown soldiers. They were disheveled and their clothes did not look very neat. Some of them were actually bare-chested. Some were wearing T-shirts or military blouses. And they acted very strange. I tried to communicate with them, to see what was going on and where the prisoners had come from, who had brought them to the elementary school. They would not talk to me about that. I insisted upon receiving information, and I used a somewhat more commanding tone in that communication, but they still refused to talk to me, and then I asked them if any of their commanders or commanding officers were there to give me information with this regard. They told me that I couldn't talk to them, that they did not have any obligation towards me. At one point, since I was rather brash in that conversation, one of those soldiers raised his rifle and pointed it in my direction. I realised at that moment that - how shall I put it? - that those soldiers were under some sort of influence, alcohol or narcotics. In any case, their behaviour was rather erratic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you personally go into the gym of the school?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not go to the gym. I entered a school-yard with the priest and the president of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see any prisoners with your own eyes while you were there at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I could hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What could you hear?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I heard shouts from the gym. People were screaming for water. They wanted to go to the bathroom. The temperatures were running very high around that time. They had certain requests, and I could hear those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the school when you went there with the president and the priest?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I suppose that that conversation and my contact with the aforementioned soldiers went on for about half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And please tell us, when you left the school, where did you go next and what did you decide to do after having seen the situation in your home village?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I went back to join my unit. From there, I was going to call the brigade command to see if they knew anything and to inform them what was going on in Rocevic. But then it occurred to me that in my former logistics unit, there was a telephone that was in Kozluk. I arrived in that office and from there I called the duty operations officer, the duty operations officer of the Zvornik Brigade, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So approximately what time would it be -- I know it was a long time ago, but roughly, when you made this phone call?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I told you that I was at the school sometime between 2000 and 2100 hours, and since I spent some 30 minutes talking to the soldiers, it could have been any time between 2030 or 2130. I suppose, I'm not sure when I had arrived there but I suppose that this would be about the right time when I made that telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know the name of the Zvornik Brigade duty officer you spoke to? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I suppose that at that very moment I knew who was on the other end, but I can't remember who it was as I sit here today. I only know that when I called him, I wanted to ask him where and how come these people were in the gym in the Rocevic school. He told me that he didn't know anything about that, and then I also lost my patience and I asked him whether he knew at all what was going on down there, and I explained to him what was going on. I told him that the people who were guarding, I suppose, a large number of soldiers, were behaving erratically, that they had wounded that woman. Then he told me, and I could recognise in his voice that he was scared, he told me that he didn't know anything about that, that he was not abreast of the situation, which made me assume that somebody was standing next to him and that he was not free to discuss that topic, and then I started shouting at him, literally shouting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I object to this witness speculating like this, reading people's minds and assuming things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's first make things clear. I don't like - and I'm sure my colleagues agree with me - interrupting the witness while he is giving testimony, unless it's a special case that needs interruption. And this certainly is not the case because the witness is not speculating. He is telling us what conclusion he came to at the time when he was on the phone with this person. This is not speculation. He may have been wrong, he may have been right, but this is -- was his feeling at the time when he was talking or speaking to this person. And of course, you can ask questions to the witness on cross-examination on whether he was speculating or not. Please don't interrupt the witness in the course of his answer unless it is absolutely imperative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, please. You were just saying how you started shouting at the duty officer. If you could you tell us what happened next in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Then I asked if the brigade commander or the Chief of Staff were there, and I insisted to be put into contact with them. But the duty officer told me that the commander was not there and neither was the Chief of Staff. I then said that if he gets in touch with either of the two, that he must tell them about what was happening in Rocevic and tell them to contact me, to call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is this when you say Chief of Staff, who are you referring to? Just for the record, can you give us the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then did you continue the conversation? Was there any more information exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I then asked if there is anyone there besides the duty officer or besides the duty officer that I could discuss this topic with in the brigade headquarters, because I realised that there was nothing he could do and I assumed, because he was telling me that he did not know what was happening, and he told me that Vujadin Popovic had arrived just at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was Vujadin Popovic's position at this time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was -- in fact, he was the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the corps, the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I explained to him what I had learned in Rocevic, and I told him what was happening down there at the school, that the soldiers were killing the prisoners in front of the school there. The school was in the centre of the village. I told him that they had no control over the situation at all, and that there could be a general disaster and tragedy, things like that. And he told me that I should not put things in such dramatic terms, that I should calm down, and that those prisoners would be exchanged the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you for one second. You've just explained a little conversation you had and you said that you told him, and -- about the situation at the school. What you've just said, are you talking about talking to the duty officer or to Officer Popovic, what you just explained?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: With Popovic. The duty officer put me through to him or rather he handed him the phone and I talked to him then, because he introduced himself to me when he talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did Mr. Popovic tell you anything else about the prisoners or what would happen other than that they would be exchanged in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did he seem surprised when you told him about the prisoners at the school?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. But since he gave me the answer that those prisoners would be exchanged the next day, so he must have known what prisoners I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do after this conversation which you were having?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we pause there, if I can interrupt? It's page 30, lines from 4 to 5, it's explanation of the witness to the duty operations officer -- to Popovic. The witness said that he had seen or the -- I'll read it. "I told him what was happening down there at the school, that the soldiers were killing the prisoners in front of the school there." I'm not sure whether the witness told us that he had seen those killings. Could you clarify with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He did not say that in his prior testimony, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you -- but we were getting to that. Could you explain, please, sir, how you got that information about prisoners being killed at the school that you relayed to Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I first got this information from the president of the local commune and the priest. They had come to talk to me because of that. That's why they came to see me in my house. And they told me that on that occasion, while those prisoners were being killed, that this woman was wounded, as I described earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you please tell us, going on through the chronology of events, what did you do next after this phone call which took place where you -- after your phone call you made from Kozluk? Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I went back to Rocevic again to tell the president of the local commune and the priest that the prisoners would be taken away to be exchanged, that they would be exchanged the next day, in order to alleviate their concerns, the concerns in the village, because there was widespread panic there because of these events that I just described, what I've just described. So I got in touch with them when I came back from Kozluk, with the president, but I told these soldiers that those prisoners would be exchanged tomorrow and that it would be good to give some water to the prisoners in the gym, and to allow them to give them what they were asking for, the things that I had heard when I was in the courtyard in front of the gym. But they didn't even want to discuss this topic at all, and they rejected this possibility out of hand. So I and the president of the local commune made the efforts again to persuade those soldiers to let the prisoners have some water and to allow them to go out and to use the toilet, or at least to give them some containers, some adequate containers that could be used for this purpose. After about 15 minutes, we reached an agreement, or, rather, they agreed that the prisoners should be given some water and that some containers should be given to them for their physical needs, and the president of the local commune stayed there to get some of those jerrycans with water and to get those containers for them and I went back to my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, can you tell us the name of the president of the local commune who you've been referring to, if you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you got back to your battalion command, what did you do? Did you have any discussions with anybody? What was going on there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I informed my close associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, as far as you remember, who you informed, what their names are, what their positions were?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think I met Vujo Lazarevic, and Mitar Lazarevic. Mitar Lazarevic was the general affairs officer, and Vujo Lazarevic was the assistant battalion commander for morale and religious affairs. I remember that I told them, and I didn't have the deputy at that time. My previous deputy had been demobilised, and the assistant for security was out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you make any reports to the Zvornik Brigade command after this second visit to the school? Or talk to anybody there?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Again, when I returned to the unit, I contacted the duty officer. I asked him again whether the commander or the Chief of Staff had arrived in the meantime. I asked to be put in contact with him. But I got similar replies as in my brief attempt, as I just described, that the Chief of Staff was not available, that he was out in the field, that they couldn't get in touch with him, things like that. And I also left a message that if they should manage to get in touch with the commander or the Chief of Staff, that they should notify me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you talk to anybody on that phone call besides the duty officer? Did you talk to anybody else at the Zvornik Brigade in the second telephone call?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to the duty officer, as I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is anybody else that you remember speaking to on the second call?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was later, when I got back. I had this conversation during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that. So just to be clear, did you -- the conversation you described with -- having with Mr. Popovic, is that the only conversation you had with him that night, with Mr. Popovic, or was there any others?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was the only time that we spoke in that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Going on through this night, after you've returned from the school the second time, did you receive any orders during the night from the Zvornik Brigade, your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What time was this that you received an order?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was before midnight -- after midnight. I think it was between 1.00 and 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe that for us, please? What orders you received, how you received them and what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And where was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought he'd said he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is while you are still back at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He said he'd gone there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's whether he was still there when he received the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were you when you received these orders or became aware of these orders around 2.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the battalion command, when we received the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And tell us what the telegram said.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: The telegram said that a platoon of soldiers should be detached, and that they should be used for the execution of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was this telegram sent from, just to be very clear?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was sent from the Zvornik Brigade, that the duty officer sent it, or somebody else who was at the Zvornik Brigade command at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this telegram, how is that received? Is that over a phone line or radio or handed by courier? How does that telegram come to you at the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: This telegram was received over the telephone but it was encrypted, the telegram was encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to receiving this telegram ordering you to put together a platoon of soldiers to be used to execute prisoners? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I was asleep, and the duty officer at the battalion command who received the telegram woke me up. I was told I should get up, I should go down. They woke me up. I went down. The telegram had already been decoded by the time I went there to the duty officer's room, and they told me about the contents of the telegram. I took the telegram, I read it. We were taken aback. We were simply flabbergasted that something like that could be asked of us. We were simply in a state of shock. We couldn't believe that something like that could be asked of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I consulted my associates, the ones that I mentioned. We said that we would not be detaching any of our personnel for that purpose. We wrote a telegram. We indicated that we don't have any personnel for that person [as interpreted] and we were also asked to inform the company commanders about the contents of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, if you could clarify with the witness whether the telegram was in the form of an order and under whose name it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you've heard His Honour's question. If you could tell us, was this telegram an order? First, did you take it as an order?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know who the person signing the telegram was or whose authority it purported it was under, if there was a name on the telegram of who was making this order to you?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I described this in my statements that I gave in Banja Luka when I was questioned there. In light of the contents of the telegram, and I've already told you what was in there, it really shocked us. So we focused on the contents of the telegram itself, and I didn't pay any attention to the signatory. I may have seen it at that time, but I simply forgot all about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question just so that the transcript is clear. You said that you sent a telegram and you indicated that: " ... we don't have personnel," and in our transcript it says, "for that person." Is that right or is it for that task or that assignment or something else? It says you didn't have any personnel for that person, in line -- page 36, line 8.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. We sent a telegram that we didn't have any personnel for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you send this telegram to?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: To the duty officer in the brigade. I think we sent it to the duty officer. Or the assistant for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you receive any response to your telegram that you had sent back to the brigade stating that men were unavailable for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: We received yet another telegram. I think it was within 45 minutes or maybe an hour. And again, the contents were the same and it was stated that personnel had to be detached for this purpose and that I should personally inform the company commanders about the contents of the telegram but I think that in this telegram, it actually did say explicitly that the company commanders should be informed about it and so, in other words, the battalion command should be informed about it and the company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do about informing the company commanders?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the telegram indicated that company commanders should be notified and that the communications section had already forwarded this telegram to the company commanders, but now it was emphasised that I personally should inform them about it. I again consulted my assistants in the battalion command, and we took a very firm stand that we would not be detaching any of our men for this purpose, and I got in touch with the company commanders and I asked them if they had received the telegram. I think I asked them if they had received the telegram. And they confirmed that, yes, they had. I explained to them what agreement we had reached at the battalion command, that we would refuse to obey this order, and I told them that I had called them just to notify them, and so that if anyone from the brigade were to check, they were to say that they had been notified and we didn't ask them to supply any personnel for this purpose, we merely notified them about the contents of the telegram. And I asked for their support, if anything should happen because of our refusal to obey this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's pause here for the time being. Now, when you say, "I again consulted my assistants in the battalion command," are you referring to the two Lazarevics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I remember that they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then when you say, "I then got in touch with the company commanders," could you tell us who they were, please? Could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragan Stjepanovic, the commander of the 1st Infantry Company for -- I'm not sure about the other two company commanders. I don't know whether I spoke to the company commanders or their assistants. I think that the commander of the 3rd Infantry Company was not there in our unit at the time, and I also think that the commander of the 2nd Infantry Company was in the field, but he was not in the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility. So I may have talked either to the company commander or to their deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please, if you remember, tell us the names of the company commanders for the 2nd and 3rd companies?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Infantry Company, Miroslav Stankovic. The 3rd Infantry Company, Milan Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after receiving this second telegram, with essentially the same orders, did you respond to that? Did you notify the brigade of your decision to -- that you would not obey that order?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: We forwarded that response back, and our response was negative as it was the time before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after sending this second telegram back, again, saying that you would not do this, did you receive any other communications from the Zvornik Brigade that night into the next morning on this subject?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you explain that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic get into contact with me using a civilian telephone line. After we had sent our negative response back, in the telegram we said that we did not have enough people for that. Then Drago Nikolic called me personally using the civilian telephone line. That line existed in the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What time did Drago Nikolic call you at the battalion command, as best you can remember, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately at 2.30. I cannot pinpoint the time. I can't say exactly what the time was at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. If you remember, and if you don't, that's fine too, but about how long was it after you had sent back the second telegram to the brigade, again refusing to take part in this?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Some ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As best you remember, what did Drago Nikolic say to you during that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: When Drago Nikolic called me, he told me that the order had to be carried out. I told him that we did not have enough people for that. And I also told him that we would not carry out the order, and I told him exactly this. "What's the matter with you? Drago, how can you ask us to do something of that sort?" This was the context of our conversation more or less. He told me that the order had come from above, using these words, and that this should be done. A platoon had to be allocated for that. He put a pressure on me. He told me that I had to carry out that order, that I could not refuse to carry out that order. Again, like the previous time, in the telegram that we had sent back to the brigade, I told him again that we did not have enough people for that and that we were not in a position to allocate anybody for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long was this conversation? As best as you can remember, how long were you on the phone with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To avoid any possible confusion, 2.30, you were talking of 2.30 at night and not 2.30 in the afternoon? 2.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This would be 2.30 in the morning after these events; is that correct, witness?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did Drago Nikolic at the end of this -- well, during this conversation, did he tell you what was going to happen next or give you any ultimatums or how did he leave it with what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: He told me again, as we were drawing our conversation to an end, that before 7.00 in the morning, we should do everything that we possibly could to allocate people for that purpose, that our deadline was 7.00 in the morning. He also told me on that occasion, as our conversation was drawing to an end, that we would speak again around 7.00 or 8.00 in the morning. His intention was to check what I had done with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you have -- what happened at 7.00 a.m.? Did you have any communication from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: At 7.00 or at 8.00, Drago called again. He asked me whether we had assigned a group of men, whether we had executed the order. I told him again, like on the other few times, that we had not and we would not assign anybody to that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you describe, as best you can, as you remember, Drago Nikolic's voice and manner while he was talking to you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: He was putting pressure on me. He was talking in high tones. As far as I can remember, he was swearing a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did he give you any advice of any kind about how to actually conduct this operation other than putting, again telling you to get the men together? Did he give you any instruction, direction or advice on what you should do to accomplish this task? You personally.

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: He told me this: "If [Realtime transcript read in error "In"] you're not capable of getting these men together, I will personally do it with my battalion command." I responded to that that I had stopped even thinking about that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At any time did he suggest to you that you should personally take part in carrying out these executions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. That's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a leading question, I don't want to interrupt but there are limits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to. We allow leading questions when there is no objection but when there is a founded objection, you either skip the question or you rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else he told you about, about this job of executing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've explained about how he said, "If you're not capable of getting these men together," I'm just asking you if you remember, did he say anything else about the way in which these executions should be carried out or what you should do personally in order to make sure they are carried out?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he wanted to put pressure on us when he told us that we should personally carry that out. He, I suppose, wanted us to be more serious about the whole thing. He wanted us to try harder in order to find men who would do it. I believe that this was what he wanted to achieve in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did he tell you to go anywhere or do anything during this conversation?

utterances.speaker: SRECKO ACIMOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of that conversation, he also told me that I should personally wait for him in the school in Rocevic at 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning. I told him then -- I asked him actually whether he was aware of the fact that I was not in a position to abandon my unit given the situation that they were -- that we were in. I reminded him of the telegrams that he -- that we had received during the night announcing an attack on the 2nd Infantry Battalion, and I also reminded him that we could expect an attack from the rear in the direction of Klisa and Boskovic, i.e., in the direction of the 2nd and the 3rd Infantry Battalions. I informed him about all that. I told him what my orders had been. I told him that I was not supposed to leave my command post because my deputy was not there, my assistant for security was not there, I was by myself literally. I was the only person in the battalion command with my two assistants. And I told him that I was not supposed to leave the command position given the situation that we were in. My defence sector had not been reinforced because we had just moved our defence line. There was a lot of confusion going on during that period of time in the entire area, in the units, that there were. In addition to all that, and despite everything that I told him, he told me that I should personally be in Rocevic. He told me that this was my order, that I should personally be there and that he would be waiting for me at either 9.00 or 10.00. Now I'm not sure whether he said 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, we need to have a break now. It will be a shorter break than usual, just 20 minutes. And then we will resume and continue until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It appears there was a translation error and an error in the transcript and I've discussed this with my colleagues, especially those who speak Serbian on the other side and they've confirmed that there was an error. This is at lines 42 -- page 42 excuse me, lines 5 to 7. The transcript reads, "He told me this: "In" - I think it should be if, if - "you're not capable of getting these men together, I will personally do it with my battalion command." What I'm told the witness said was, "If you're not capable of getting these men together, you should personally do it with your battalion command." In other words, that Mr. Nikolic did not say that he would personally come down but that the witness should personally do it with his men from the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me first ask the witness whether he confirms this. Mr. Acimovic, do you confirm that this is what you actually stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat all that so that I can answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll go through it myself. While you are testifying in your own language, we are receiving interpretation either in English or in French. It's being suggested that a part of what you said has been wrongly translated to us. What we have in the transcript -- what we have in the transcript is supposedly wrong. What we have in the transcript is as follows: That while you were on the phone with Drago Nikolic, he told you, if you are not capable of getting these men together, I will personally do it with my battalion. Mr. Nikolic [sic] is suggesting that this is not what you actually said but. What you said you heard Mr. Nikolic telling you was if you are not capable of getting these men together, then you will -- you should personally do it with your battalion command. Is that what you actually said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
